I do not propose this afternoon to refer to all the things that have been said, because most of these questions were fully discussed in the veterans affairs committee. I want to say, first of all, that I and the officials of my department realize fully that these matters affecting veterans are unfinished business and will remain unfinished business long after the end of this session, even if Canada should not take part in any more wars.
The discussion this afternoon has ranged about two items connected with the bill. One is the amount of the increase. The other is eligibility: the eligibility of those who served in Britain only in the first war; and secondly, the eligibility of the British Canadian veterans who came to Canada after the old war and resided in Canada for many years but who was not resident in Canada prior to his service in 1914. The arguments on that have been discussed here and elsewhere. I am not going to say that the increase we have provided in the bill is such as any member of the veterans affairs committee or any member of this house would like to see, but I would point out that since 1930 the War Veterans Allowance Act has been twice improved in that respect. It was $20 in 1930 and stands at $40 today for the single man, and $70 for the married man. The government felt, in a year when the pensions bill had been increased, the first increase since 1926, that the committee had incorporated in this bill a reasonable increase which is looked upon as a permanent increase. We are now at a peak time as to both cost of living and employment. It is true, as has been stated this afternoon, that the older veterans cannot all get work; nevertheless a surprisingly large proportion of them are working, a great many of them full-time and many of them part-time. They are anxious to work, and I doubt whether many of them will give up useful and interesting works just to keep themselves within the terms

War Veterans Allowance Act
of the amount which will be applicable to them under these amendments.
We should also bear in mind that there must be some equitable relationship between the benefits under this act and the benefits granted to those old people who did not serve Canada in uniform in the early days of their lives. As it is now, leaving out of consideration for the moment a very special factor, the terms of this act by and large- I am not going to argue the details this afternoon-are as good as those of any old age pension scheme in any province of Canada. But the special factor which I mentioned is that under this bill the old soldier at the age of sixty, if he comes within its terms, automatically gets war veterans allowance at the age of sixty rather than at the age of seventy, as is the case with old age pensions.
On the point of eligibility of members of the Canadian forces who served only in England during the first war, I think it is evident from the discussion here this afternoon that, if at this time they were made eligible under this bill, right behind it comes the next point:	What about those who served only
in Canada for four or five years in the first war? Side by side with that comes another point: What about the second war and those who served only in Canada? You have those questions raised right there. It is but dodging the issue to say these are not so vocal. I think, before that bridge is crossed, some decision must be reached. I think, too, the generation of veterans who are still young, and who served only in Canada, in the second war, might give some consideration to looking forward in years to come to an equitable protection through the normal social security measures within our country.
On the third point I state right now that I should like to consider all the factors which have been submitted in the discussion this afternoon and to keep it under consideration for the future.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ET CETERA
speechtext: There is one other point I should like to have perfectly clear, namely, the ceiling on the combined income allowed to a burnt-out pensioner. I recognize that, at the moment, 1 am not looking at the fact that casual income is outside the pale. Apart from that, the bill as it went to the committee provided in the case of single veterans for an allowance of $365 and $250 other income, or a total ceiling of $615 a year. The bill as it has come back from the committee provides for an allowance of $485 and other income of $125, or a ceiling of $610. In other words, there has been an actua1 reduction of $5 a year in the ceiling on allowance and other income. The corresponding figures for a married burnt-out pensioner are as follows: The bill as it went to the committee provided for an allowance of $730, and $375 other income permissible, or a total of $1,105. The bill as we now have it before us provides for an allowance of $850. and other income of $250, or a total of $1,100. The amount involved is small, only $5 a year, but it does seem strange that this reduction should have been made. How it comes about is that the allowance has been increased by $120 a year, and the amount of other income allowed has been reduced by $125 a year. Basically I strongly support the point made by the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough that the amount of other income should be put back to $250. I remind the government again that that is what they found they had to do with respect to the old age pension question back in 1943 and 1944. But at the moment I should like to have this reduction of $5 clarified.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ET CETERA
speechtext:
I am rather averse to going into the intricacies of this. All I can do is to assure the hon. member that the object sought by the committee with regard to that angle of it, at any rate, has been achieved. It will be remembered that in the original draft of the bill the expression used was "supplementary allowance of $10 a month". That then was a separate item. Then, when the parliamentary committee got at it they said, why do you call it a supplementary allowance? There was no reason, because it was intended that it should be permanent, anyway. Therefore it was lifted from there over to another clause. I am assured by the

deputy minister that it conveys the desire of the committee on that score, and that the thing which is desired to be done is being done. The permissible income remains the same.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ET CETERA
speechtext: I should like to follow up what the hon. member for Nanaimo said regarding the amount of the pension. I hope that the minister will give consideration to the men of the first war who were not allowed to leave Britain. I have a typical case in my own constituency. This man went overseas in the early part of the war, in 1914. He was among the first to go over. He was employed in instructing officers in gas warfare. I am sure that the hon. member remembers those days. That man was not allowed to leave Britain. He is now back home. He has lived in Canada all his life. He is refused a pension because he was not out of Britain. I think the minister will probably admit that this is a deserving case, and there may be more than one.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ET CETERA
speechtext: I should like to point out to the minister that in both clauses 3 and 4 these words are used: "Without child or children." Both the single and the plural are used. I take it that this means that a widow or widower, whether he or she has one child or six children would receive the same amount of allowance. The allowance would be exactly the same. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ET CETERA
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ET CETERA
speechtext: If that is correct, does the minister not think a widower with more than one child should have a permissible income of more than $250 a year?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ET CETERA
speechtext: I cannot very well answer the question offhand as to whether I consider it adequate. I do not think the item has been challenged by the committee, and I should like to see it carried as it is.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ET CETERA
speechtext: In the Pension Act there is a separate allowance for each child. Apparently the War Veterans Allowance Act does not recognize more than one child. The amount of the allowance is exactly the same. I am not quarrelling with that; but the widower is restricted as to the amount of money that he can earn without reducing his war veterans allowance. Surely a widower with several children should be allowed to earn more than $250 a year without having his veterans allowance reduced. I do not think anybody would question that.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ET CETERA
speechtext: I should like to point out that, compared with pensions, quite a different principle is involved here. In the case of old age pensions, there is no arrangement in any of the provinces for children. This is not intended to be more than some assistance for the veteran who needs it at that particular period of his life, and it is fair to state that there are not a great many who would come under that section owing to their age.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ET CETERA
speechtext: That may be true, but you should recognize the liability, because you are providing that a widow with a child shall get double the amount. If you recognize it for one child it is only reasonable to recognize it for the other children,

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ET CETERA
speechtext: I cannot see why these men should not be allowed to earn a little extra money. Two cases were brought to my attention last week. One man drew the burnt-out pension and he could do some light work. He has two children; his wife has been ill for some time, and he advises me that it is actually impossible for him to get by on the allowance he is receiving, being allowed to earn only $250 in the year. I urge the minister to give further consideration to this provision.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ET CETERA
speechtext: If a man with a 50 per cent pensionable disability dies of that disability his widow receive $840?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ET CETERA
speechtext: The question the hon. gentleman asks relates to disability pensions. Under the War Veterans Allowance Act, it is not a question of degree of disability, since it is not strictly a pension in that sense but a living allowance. Therefore the question has no application to this specific act.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ET CETERA

If a man has a disability of 50 per cent or more, his widow will receive the whole $850. I think that is correct. Therefore a deadline is struck at 50 per cent. Why that is done no one seems to know. If a man has a 45 per cent disability which is pensionable, and he dies, the widow receives $485. I do not see why there should be

War Veterans Allowance Act
that difference. My suggestion is that further consideration should be given this point. At the present time $40 a month is about the equivalent of $20 before the war, so that there is no increase. I am making a plea for these women. They are all getting older, especially those from the last war. First of all, the deadline was 80 per cent. If the disability was over 80 per cent the widow automatically got the pension. Gradually that was lowered to 50 per cent. I do not know why that figure was decided upon. The widow whose husband had a 50 per cent disability is in the same category as the widow whose husband's disability was 45 per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ET CETERA

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ET CETERA
speechtext: The difference between $850 and $485 is considerable. The amount of the allowance at the present time is only $40 a month, which is no more than the equivalent of $20 a month before the war. As regards both the burnt-out pensioner and the widow, it would be only a small matter for the government to bring the allowance up to $50 a month. The minister has referred to old age pensions, but that has nothing to do with the maiter. The widow's husband when overseas suffered a certain degree of disability, and she looked after him. Some consideration should be given her. It would not hurt the dominion if the amount were increased to $50. The amount the veteran is allowed to earn is also ridiculously low when one considers the cost of living. I know of one veteran who can earn a bit more than $250. He is suffering from silicosis and cannot work all the time. He is a stone worker and that is all he gets, so that his income for the year is very small. Something should be done to increase these allowances.

In many cases I do not think the veteran would wish to do that. I think he would wish to feel that he was getting his pension from the source from which he had earned it, instead of transferring to another source.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ET CETERA

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ET CETERA

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ET CETERA

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR NEGLECTED OR DEPENDENT CHILDREN, INCREASED PERMISSIBLE INCOMES, ET CETERA

Mr. Chairman,I shall give my reason for the amendment. The Indian Affairs committee, which is a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons, has considered the question of voting by the Indian population in Canada. On or about May 6 of this year a unanimous report was made by the committee to the house, recommending that votes be given to the Indians on the same basis as they are given to urban voters. The reason was that in that way it would be necessary that they be enumerated and be on the enumerators' list. At elections they would not be able to go to the polls with some other person already on the list, and be sworn in.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as we
adjourned for the dinner recess I had explained that this amendment is the result of a report made to this house by the Indian affairs committee on or about the 6th day of May of this year, recommending that the North American Indian on a reserve in Canada be given the right to vote in dominion elections on the same basis as voters in urban centres. The Indian would then have to be enumerated and be on an enumerator's list on election day. This recommendation was the result of many representations made to the committee by various organizations from coast to coast throughout Canada and by many Indian organizations. Representations have also been made by one who, as I speak here tonight, is sitting in the gallery of this house, the Reverend Doctor Peter Kelly, of the Native Brotherhood of British Columbia, a Doctor of Divinity and a member of the United Church clergy.
The Indian pays taxes. He pays sales tax; he pays income tax on income earned off the reserve; in fact, he pays all taxes except taxes on the land he occupies on the reserve. It is therefore felt by the Indians that they are paying taxes and having no representation. The principle of taxation without representation does not appeal to them or to many church and other organizations. It was unanimously felt by the committee that the giving of the vote to the Indian would create in him a desire to help himself-the theme of the Indian affairs committee since its inception has been that we were endeavouring to help the Indian help himself-and that it would create in the Indian a sense of obligation to society. It would train him in our democratic practices and make him realize that he has a place in the Canadian economy and in the Canadian society.
On the other hand, the giving of the vote to the Indian would result in a- recognition by government agencies and by members of parliament that the Indian was not a chattel but a human being and as such had certain rights in our society and that he should be looked to and his rights be protected. In other words, the thought of the committee has been that the giving of the vote to the Indian will help us to assimilate the Indian. When I say assimilate I do not mean that the Indian would lose his rich background of cultural achievements, or any of the rights that he enjoys under treaties, or any of his rights, statutory or at common law; but that he would be recognized as being a human being and subject to the attention of those seeking office.
This thought of the Indian affairs committee and this recommendation are not without precedent, for in the United States the vote was given to the Indian in federal elections with certain minor qualifications. So that in moving this amendment, Mr. Chairman, I feel that a great step would be taken toward the assimilation of the Indian into the population of the Dominion of Canada, and it would make not only Indians but the other Canadians realize that we are all united.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to second the amendment of the hon. member for Essex West, who, as the committee knows, was chairman of the Indian affairs committee, I think it is well to call attention at once to the recommendation that was submitted to the house last year by the Indian affairs committee in regard to the

Dominion Elections Act
enfranchisement of Indians. Perhaps I should not say "enfranchisement," because the Indians feel that there is some liability connected with that term; shall I say, grant the privilege to the Indian of voting in a federal election.
I can well appreciate the stand now taken by the Indians. They feel that they are unjustly taxed by the income tax law, because they say they have not a vote. Generally speaking, it is the more advanced and more cultured Indians who will be paying most of the tax, because in ordinary circumstances the more cultured among them have the higher incomes.
When the Indian affairs committee made this recommendation we knew that the committee on the Dominion Elections Act was sitting, and I thought at that time it would be possible for that committee to consider our recommendation and make it possible for certain segments of our Indian population, the better educated and more advanced, to vote in dominion elections. Everyone will agree that the problem of Indians voting is a peculiar one. We have 125.000 Indians scattered over this country from the United States border to the Arctic ocean, and as a result they are bound to be in all stages of civilization. The more advanced professional people among the Indians live near the United States border, and the Indians who are still in almost an aboriginal state live farther north. I do not think it would be wise to grant to the aboriginal native Indian, without an education and without a knowledge of English, the same privilege that we grant to his brother who may be a professional man. That is the feeling of the Indian leaders themselves. They realize what a vast difference there is in the culture of the Indians in various parts of Canada.
As a way out of some part of the problem, it seems to me that it might be necessary for us to recommend to the committee on the Dominion Elections Act that an Indian applying for the privilege of voting be required to fill in an application to indicate to the enumerators that he can read and write. It does not seem quite right that a man who cannot read the names on the ballot should have the privilege and the responsibility of going into an election booth and taking part in a federal election. There is no question that the educational disability which some of the Indians possess will be overcome in the next twenty years so far as seventy-five per cent of them are concerned. Anybody who has studied the program of the Department of Mines and Resources and the Department of National Health and Welfare will realize that these branches of government are making available 
a greater sum of money to further Indian educational advancement. From my own personal knowledge of the Indians on the Pacific coast, I would say that within the next twenty years most of them will be competent to exercise an intelligent franchise without any test as to education. In fact, most of them are competent now. The difficulties and problems which the Indians now face will certainly be solved by the action of the members of parliament whom, I trust, they will help to elect when they receive the vote.

The committee considered the act last session and throughout this session, d he amendment which has been put forward tonight is not one that was brought before the committee during its meeting, and while I do not know all the problems that it would raise,
I understand that many Indians are not anxious to have the vote. I understand that in Saskatchewan the chiefs of all the tribes in that province at a gathering decided to have a petition forwarded that they be not granted the vote, since they felt it might be the thin edge of the wedge to take away their treaty rights. I believe this matter should be thoroughly considered by the elections committee before being incorporated in the act, and I would suggest that the amendment be dropped in the meantime and referred to the elections committee at another session, so that it could be given careful consideration.

I am in favour of allowing the Indians to vote, because they should be citizens. I refer to those who did not serve in the first and second wars. Citizenship should be made available to them.
I should like to refer to a matter which I voted for before, namely, subsection 1, paragraph (k), which refers to those in charitable institutions. They have borne the heat of the day, and many of them have voted all their lives. I am in favour of extending this provision, notwithstanding the provision in some of the other provincial acts.

speechtext: I should like to say a few words in support of this amendment. I have the pleasure of representing the largest Indian reserve in the Dominion of Canada, and am also a member of the Indian Affairs committee. In view of the minister's remarks, surely we can accept the recommendation of the Indian Affairs committee, which has been meeting now for the past three years, without sending this amendment back to the elections act committee. I would be very sorry if that were done. The Indians were the first citizens of this country.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: Surely it is time that these people were allowed the privilege of voting if they wish. I realize that many Indians do not wish to vote. Why is that? Because they are fearful that, by so doing, they will lose part of their rights and privileges. That is not true. Indians are a very proud people. They do not want to lose their identity as Indians. If we pass this amendment now we shall not be forcing them to vote. We shall simply be giving them an opportunity to vote if they wish. I think it would be poor judgment on the part of this committee not to pass this amendment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER

I should like to say one or two words on this amendment. To me it is a surprising amendment. I was a member of the elections act committee. At no time was there a suggestion before our committee that the Indian should get the vote. In my own riding I have over forty Indian reserves. The Indian question is very much to the fore. To me, and I think to the leaders of the Indian groups in my riding, the solution of the Indian problem of Canada is to get the Indians away from being wards of the government and living on reserves, to the ordinary everyday rights of Canadian citizens living in cities, municipalities and districts, paying normal taxes and voting as Canadians. Therefore I cannot see how Indians who still want to maintain their treaty rights as wards of the state living on reserves away from the great influence of Canadian life can expect at the same time to be able to vote as Canadian citizens in dominion elections.
I confess that for the first time since I have been in the House of Commons I am at odds with my very good friend-we use that word very loosely around the House of Commons -the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. With all due deference, for example, to the hon. member for Davenport, I doubt whether there is a member in this House of Commons who knows the Indians of Canada as well as 5849-335
the hon. member for Comox-Alberni does. He was pretty well reared in an Indian village. His west coast riding of Comox-Alberni includes more Indians. I suppose, than the rest of British Columbia, who are renowned in Canadian history, the most warlike of all the Canadian Indians, the only ones who stopped the Spanish, the British and the Canadian explorers. But at the same time I wonder, when the hon. member for Comox-Alberni asks for the vote for the Indians, whether he would turn his mind back to two or three years ago and think whether some of these old klootchmen-that is an Indian phrase on the west coast-whether these very old and aged Indian women, if called upon at the last election to sort out the relative virtues of Jack Gibson, the Independent candidate for parliament, Nigel Morgan, the communist candidate for parliament and Mr. Barnett, C.C.F. candidate for parliament, because of their lack of knowledge of the English or the French language-they speak Chinook-could have decided which one of these three was best able to represent them in parliament,

I feel that one of the great incentives in the way of getting the Indians off the reserves, so that they might live as the rest of Canadians do under normal circumstances, would be to say to them, "if you cease being wards of the government, if you move out of the reserve and live as other Canadians live, you will get the vote". That would be a great incentive to the Indians.
Dominion Elections Act

In my own riding I live three blocks away from one of the principal reserves in the Vancouver area. In my own city of North Vancouver there are a great number of Indian families-as a matter of fact one cannot call them Indian families; they are Canadian families-who left the reserve to establish themselves where their children would go, not to Catholic or to Protestant Indian schools, but to Canadian schools, where they would learn to live as Canadians. These people have the vote. I should like to think they will vote for me, but whether they vote for me or for my opponent, they have established that right. I say therefore that, because those hon. members who are interested in this matter evidently did not take sufficient interest in it to bring it before the committee on the elections act, and secondly, because those who still live on the reserves are wards of the government and as such are dependents and not entitled to the consideration which should be given to Indians who have left their reserves and begun to live as Canadians, I must vote against the amendment moved by the hon. member for Essex West and seconded by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
I welcome the opportunity of supporting the amendment moved by the chairman of the Indian affairs committee, and I am particularly impressed by the seconder, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, and even more so after the recommendation he received from the hon. member from Vancouver North. I feel, therefore, that I am on solid ground when I suggest to the committee, agreeing with the mover of the resolution, that the time has come for us, not only to consider the discontinuance of the practice, but actually to put an end to it, of treating the Indians like children. Let us, instead, allow them to live normal adult lives.
I recall the debate in this house on a resolution moved by the hon. member for Calgary East in 1945 when many pious utterances were made over the usual period of an hour, but nothing has been done in the three years that have elapsed. My own feeling is that we have too long kept the Indians in dependence and restricted them to an inferior status. The time has come-it should not be twenty years hence; the time is now-when we should clothe them with the dignity of citizenship and assimilate them into Canadian life. I think our difficulty has been that we have adopted a paternal attitude toward the Indians; as a matter of fact, an attitude of archaic paternalism which belongs to another day.
Whether this committee believes it or not, the Indian is the only man without a vote in

the country of his origin. I am told that in the last war 5,000 Indians served in the armed forces.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER

I am not suggesting that they did not. In this war there were 4,000. They also pay taxes. I think that should appeal to hon. members when they realize that taxation without representation changed the face of the continent to the south of us.
The suggestion is made that Indians are a backward race. That is due to sheer neglect and indifference on our part. Instead of the Indians being backward, our treatment of the Indian marks us as backward at the present time. I welcome this discussion, because it is an opportunity to correct a great wrong. It is a reform long overdue. I do not think the resolution went far enough. It is time that the Indian affairs committee reported, so that we might have an Indian department with Indians on the staff, giving the Indians an opportunity to lead normal lives. Canadian Indians must become Canadian citizens. Eor that reason I support the resolution.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext: I should like to support the motion made by the hon. member for Essex West. I am unable to understand why anyone would like to continue to keep the Indians in a class by themselves as the only people born in this country who have not the right to vote. A man coming from any other part of the world, after fulfilling his residence qualification, has the right to vote, and his children born here have the right to vote, regardless of their understanding of the election issues or anything else in that regard. I cannot see why we should continue to keep this one group of people in the position where they are denied the franchise. The situation is anomalous, in that all Indians who are veterans have the right to vote, so that on some reservations, of people with more or less the same educational qualifications and understanding of national affairs, some may vote, while others have not the right. I submit that the time is long past when these people should be granted the same rights in respect of the franchise which everyone else in the country enjoys.

Mr. Chairman, I understand that this is the clause under which it would be appropriate to make the few remarks I desire to make with respect to the method of taking the vote. Suggestions have been made from time to time by influential groups in this country representing serious-minded people who have given a great deal of consideration to the study of the method of voting. I am one of those who are desirous of having the single transferable vote adopted in constituencies where more than two candidates are running.
I come from a province where the single transferable vote has been used in provincial elections for a considerable number of years. In my view and in the view of many others the results have been good, in that they have eliminated the election of members by a minority vote in the riding. This does not introduce a new method of voting, because it is the practice also in the province of Alberta. Here again I am told that the results have been satisfactory to the electors.
One need only to look at the membership of this house as it has been brought up to date in the last few days to realize the extent to which minority representation exists. At the present time there are 145 members who are in this house as a result of minority votes in the ridings from which they come. I admit quite freely, as someone will no doubt point out, that in the last election that condition applied to myself. Some sixty of those members are members of the government party; thirty-eight are members of the Progressive Conservative party; twenty-eight are members of the C.C.F. party; twelve are members of the Social Credit party, and there are seven others. If we needed lessons, we have had additional lessons in connection with this matter in the last few weeks.
Surely this is an opportune time to raise the question and) to invite hon. members to give serious consideration to it. A few moments ago the Secretary of State indicated that he did not desire to reopen a question and refer it back to the committee, but if I heard him correctly he did indicate that such matters as this committee might desire to have discussed further before another election, assuming that there would not be one in the interval between sessions, could be referred back to the committee.
This is a matter which has been exercising the minds of large numbers of people in this country over a considerable period of years. It has been supported by a large section of the party of which I am a member since as far
Dominion Elections Act

back as 1921, 1925, 1926 and consistently since. It was supported in the house in my time enthusiastically by the C.C.F. party, although it is notable that, since that party achieved power in the one place in which they have achieved it, namely Saskatchewan, they have been cold to the idea, and have tended to veer toward the support of another form of voting known as proportional representation, in which I do not desire to support them.
I wish to make it abundantly clear that my plea with respect to this is for the single transferable vote. It will be urged against the adoption of this practice that in the large majority of cases where this practice is followed there has been very little change in the representation as between the candidate who was high on the first count and the candidate who ultimately won on the second count.
I have not done the necessary research to discover the exact number of cases in which this situation has obtained in either ALberta or Manitoba, where the practice is followed; but I suggest this to the committee, that even if that be true, and even if it should prove to be an almost universal practice that the candidate who was high on the first count was ultimately elected, it does not remove one of the principal arguments for the adoption of the single transferable vote. The point is this, that the man who is high on the first count, or the man who is second on the first count, in the event of there being three candidates, does have the satisfaction of knowing that when he rises in his place in a legislature, or in the House of Commons, he is there or here by virtue of the fact that a majority of the electors in that constituency preferred him on either their first or their second choice, to speak for them. This system eliminates something of the disquietude of mind which disturbs the constituents themselves, when they realize that under the present system the man who is elected may have a majority opposed to him; and yet he speaks in their name.
It will remove that feeling; and if it did nothing else it would be worthy of consideration because of the added confidence it would give to the electors under our system of representative government, in the conviction that they have indeed a full share in electing the person who speaks for them in the legislatures of the country.
I am not going to branch out into a dissertation as to the methods or practices in connection with the system. I suggest through you, Mr. Chairman, to the committee, that there has never been a time more opportune than the present for the serious consideration of a change in our electoral law.

I expect there are those who are allergic to change. No doubt there are some among us who might have in their ridings and in their own personalities opposition and objection to change. However, this is something which I should hope would recommend itself to members of the house for serious study. We shall have an interval between now and the next session-I do not expect a very long interval- and during that time if we have any sort of assurance that when the house convenes again a committee will be set up to give further study to the matter, I would earnestly hope that members w'ould give this matter some further thought.

Coming from the most progressive province in Canada, Alberta, I wish to support the stand taken by the hon. member for Winnipeg South. I am sorry he did not go much farther. However, perhaps he has many other things on his mind, since his elevation recently to a new post, upon which we all congratulate him. Because I am so firmly convinced that the single transferable vote is what we should have, I intend to move an amendment which will bring the single transferable vote into effect, provided that it gets the necessary support in the House of Commons.
Therefore, before going farther I move, seconded by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), another Alberta member who is proud of his province:
That subsection 3 of section 45 be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"In single member constituencies the elector on receiving the ballot paper shall forthwith proceed into one of the polling compartments and there mark his ballot paper with a black lead-pencil in the following manner:
(a) by placing Arabic numeral 1 in the white space containing the name of the candidate of his first choice;
Ob) by placing Arabic numeral 2 in the white space containing the name of the candidate of his second choice; and,
(c) by placing Arabic numerals 3, 4, 5, etc., in the white space containing the names of the candidates of 3rd, 4th, 5th, etc., choices, until a numeral choice has been made for each candidate's name appearing on the ballot.
The elector shall then fold his ballot paper as directed so that the initials on the track of it, and the numbers on the counterfoil can be seen wdthout opening it, and hand the paper

Dominion Elections Act
to the deputy returning officer who shall, without unfolding it, ascertain by examination of the initials and numbers appearing thereon that it is the same paper as that delivered to the elector, and if the same he shall forthwith, in full view of the voter and all others present, remove and destroy the counterfoil and deposit the ballot in the ballot box."
I feel that the use of our vote is one of the most important things with which we have to deal. If we insist upon using it wrongly it does not reflect great credit upon us. In Alberta I have not heard one objection to this system of voting, although in other provinces where the system is not understood as well as it is in my province there may be objections.
However, this is a simple and handy method of getting the number of votes for a candidate. We have, for instance, four candidates running in an election none of whom receives 50 per cent of the votes. In that event the candidate receiving the low number of the votes is dropped from the count, and his second choices are distributed among the three candidates remaining. After this is done and the votes are again counted, if none of the three candidates receives 51 per cent of the votes, or 50 per cent plus one, then the next lowest man is dropped, and in like manner his second choices are distributed among numbers 1 and 2. By this method either number 1 or 2 will have better than 50 per cent of the votes.
As pointed out by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, 61 per cent of the members elected to this house represent their constituencies by minority votes. In my opinion that is not good enough. We can bring about fair representation by adoption of the single transferable vote.
I do not intend to take up more time this evening, because I expect that there will be further discussions of the matter. I should hope that, before another general election is held, this method might be put into effect.

I doubt if one could find any body of public opinion in the two central provinces to support such a complicated system of voting. It is all right for one of the parliamentary assistants and for the hon. member for Calgary West to support it. I do not object to that, or to his seconding the amendment; but the average citizen in an industrial province does not want any such system as is proposed here.
They would not have it in municipal affairs. The municipalities would go bankrupt under such a system.
The Conservative party to which I belong-
I have been nothing but a Conservative; I do not claim to be Progressive, because calling yourself "Progressive" does not make you progressive. I am true blue. I may be the only one left, and we used to have a party in this house which occupied the treasury benches.
You have union government in Manitoba and British Columbia. I can never understand our party sacrificing all our principles for four or five jobs in a union government. Sir John A. Macdonald, our leader, adopted and followed a policy of protection ever since we were a country, and Laurier followed it too. What was that policy? It was the policy of protection, bonuses, subventions and subsidies, for all the provinces. It was that policy which made this country great. Today in Manitoba and British Columbia the only alternative to union government is hon. gentlemen to my left who believe in the socialist doctrine first, last and all the time. No wonder the two old parties were beaten in Yale, Vancouver Centre and all that kind of thing.
We have no right to pass legislation such as this. You are handed a ballot, and what do you find, under this amendment? You go into a polling compartment to mark your ballot paper in the following manner:
(a) by placing Arabic numeral 1 in the white space containing the name of the candidate of his first choice.
I would start at the other end. I would not vote for any of them under such a system.
I would throw them all out. It may be all right for new settlers in some districts, but those who have been here for many years and whose ancestors have been here for two and three hundred years do not want this kind of thing. So far as I am concerned, I am utterly opposed to the proposed doctrine of the transferable vote. It would mean that you would have a system of minorities established in this country. It would be far better to go back to the provincial law in federal elections.
The other day we had a taste of what happens when you link up provincial and municipal affairs. Toronto is an industrial city, built up by protection. I have always had support from the working classes in every election, and I have practically no organization. In the last election I did not even have a car on election day except my own, to visit the polling booths. They might have stuffed the ballot boxes. They did once. Several hundred
Dominion Elections Act

ballots were found in a box in one polling subdivision where there were only fifty-seven voters. If you want a system like that, all well and good. We can blame ourselves in this house for all these new doctrines that have been introduced here. No wonder on June 7 last some of the industrial ridings in Toronto voted the way they did. I can tell you why they did. A party that stands by its principles will never lack for a leader or a policy. That is the trouble in this country. Instead of a policy of principle and progress, we have now a policy of peanuts and party. That is what we have.
To come back to the amendment, people walk into a polling compartment and vote under this complicated system. I have read (a). Then there is (b):
(b) by placing Arabic numeral 2 in the white space containing the name of the candidate of his second choice; and

Then (c);
, (c) by placing Arabic numerals 3, 4, 5, etc., in the white space containing the names of the candidates of 3rd, 4th, 5th, etc., choices, until a numerical choice has been made for each candidate's name appearing on the ballot.
I doubt if anybody understands it. We have had enough of that kind of thing, filling out our income tax forms. The other day I was told by my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works that he could not read my writing and that I should write in block letters as you do in writing your name on the income tax form.
I doubt if anybody understands this proposed system of voting; but if that is what you want, all well and good. The party that sticks to its principles will never lack a following. We did not stick to our principles in the last election, and the result was that we crucified our party principle of preferential trade like a thief in the night and hanged it on the sour apple tree.
Under this proposed system of voting, everybody who votes will need a secretary. It reminds me of the committee of forty in Toronto. They would come to the police commission, of which I was the head, and complain of some actor or actress; it was generally an actress who did not wear enough clothing. They had their sleeves too short and other things too short. We had two committees in those days, the committee of forty and the committee of one hundred. Colonel Denison asked me once, as chairman of the police commission, what the difference was between the two committees, and I told him the difference was sixty. There were sixty more wanting their pet theories than the other committee of forty. With sixty people in a committee there is more conflict than there is with forty, and there is more conflict with a committee of one hundred 
than there is with a committee of sixty. The committee of one hundred wanted to abolish the bar and save the boy, and they wound up later by forgetting all about the boy.
It would take a Philadelphia lawyer to read the ballot. Suppose I do not like candidate A. I cross him out immediately, because he is one of the block system of candidates. Then I come to (b) and I am supposed to place a numeral in the white space containing the name of the candidate of my second choice. Well, now, they had a bill up here the other night introduced by an hon. member from the province of Alberta. The hon. member for Danforth is not in the house at the moment. By that bill they were cutting up horsemeat to be eaten. I said at the time that probably there would be no horses left; no horses for my good friend, the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe, to ride around the tracks or at the Woodbine. If that is the kind of system you want, all very well.
Then we come to (c), which asks us to place numerals 3, 4, 5 and so forth in the white space containing the names of the candidates. Having seen some of these people going in to vote and requiring somebody in the polling booth at the same time to mark the ballot for them in West Centre, Toronto, where I was a candidate at one time, and having seen them go in behind the white curtain, may I say that they did not know what they were doing. Then they came out and people tried to explain to them what it was that they vot,ed for. It may be that they voted for No. 5 instead of No. 4, or No. 3 or No. 2 or No. 1. It is no wonder that a large number of ballots were found in the boxes, probably hundreds instead of twenty.
I am absolutely opposed to that kind of business. I am absolutely opposed to this modem combination system. A great many people have come to this country recently. We are glad to have them all from every country, but they will not understand this chartered accountant system. I venture to say that if this amendment should be passed the proposal should be referred by the Minister of Justice to the Supreme Court of Canada under the Supreme Court Act to find out whether this parliament has any right, over the heads of the provinces involved, to adopt such a system as the single transferable vote.

I was quite interested in the alacrity with which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre raised a point of order on this matter. I am sure he did not have in mind the fact that if it came to a vote, in view of the policy of his party in Saskatchewan, he would find some difficulty in voting on the question.
I would point out, sir, that this matter has been before the house on many occasions. ^ It goes back to the year 1923 when a resolution was passed in this house in favour of the adoption of the single transferable vote. On April 30, 1925, the Prime Minister gave assurance that a bill would be brought down, and to use his words he said, "and we will proceed with it." That was a bill for the purpose of bringing in the single transferable vote. Indeed, the late Mr. Lapointe did introduce a bill on May 26, 1925, to provide for this type of voting. It received first reading. On June 9 of that year the late Mr. Robert Forke made inquiry regarding this matter. The house was prorogued on June 27 and the matter did not proceed any further that session.
There was an election in October, 1925. On September 29, 1932, the present Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition, spoke in the Huron South by-election. According to the press reports of that date, he stated that the Liberal party advocated the alternative vote in single member constituencies, and the adoption of proportional representation in double member constituencies. In that by-election the present Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition, promised this electoral reform as an integral part of the* policy of his party.
In the election of 1935, as you remember, sir, the Prime Minister, as leader of the opposition, repeatedly committed his party to electoral reform, and on August 2 of that year he said,: "The Liberal party stands for electoral laws which will ensure true parliamentary representation of the Canadian people." I hate to take up the time of the committee to do it, but I imagine it has to be done. Nothing new has been put forward tonight in connection with the matter of voting. There is nothing new in the request to try to change the voting system. In many countries for many years they appointed commissions and committees, numbers of them. England appointed three altogether; France appointed two, Ontario appointed two. I could go throughout the world, and give the numbers. In Australia the federal government appointed two, and New' South Wales also appointed two. They were trying to ascertain some way to change from the present system of voting, which some people call the first past the post voting system, but which is ordinarily rightfully called the majority system.
Other countries have tried other systems. And, just so that the record will be straight, I should like to mention a few of the voting systems. England, Spain and Portugal, following the year 1867, tried to obtain what the hon. member for Winnipeg South likes to allege the alternative vote does; that is, obtain a majority of the votes. It does nothing of the kind, as I shall show in a moment or two.
They adopted and tried out what is called the limited vote in three-member or five-member ridings, set up purposely to try out the system. The limited vote meant that a voter could not vote for three, but that he could vote only for two. Or, in a five-member riding he could not vote for five, but could vote only for four. The vote was limited. So that there was no such thing as plumping for five or three, as the case may be. In each of those countries the limited vote system was abolished, because it was found unsatisfactory.
The next system tried out was called the cumulative vote. That is now in operation in the state of Illinois. That is the only state in the American union which uses that style of voting. It was adopted there, so that the different nationalities, of which there are many in the city of Chicago, should have representation in the local legislature. For instance, in that city there are thousands of coloured people, Italians, Poles, Russians and others.
In the state of Illinois the state elects three members to the legislature, from each electoral district. You can give the whole three votes to one, if you like, or you can give one candidate two votes and another candidate one vote, or you can give the three candidates one vote each. That is the only place in the world, I believe, where that system is used. It gives satisfaction, so far as minority representation is concerned.
The next system is one which was tried in Colorado. It is called the Bucklin system, which is a point system. There again you have a number of preferences, and if no one candidate obtains more than 50 per cent on the first count, they count the ballots over again and
Dominion Elections Act

give each candidate his first, second and third votes, and so on. Those are added together, and whoever gets the highest total votes gets the seat. That has been abolished in nearly every place in which it has been tried in the western United States, and that is the only place it was tried.
Then, in Europe they have tried what is called the second ballot. Theoretically the second ballot is the best of all of them; but in actual operation it does not work out satisfactorily. Besides that, there are two systems of it. The second ballot was tried in quite a number of European countries. France tried it. There are two different systems. Under one system, if an election was held on the 10th of the month in single member ridings and no one candidate in a riding obtained a majority, then a second ballot was held ten days later. The voters are asked to vote for all1 the candidates over again; only in the second ballot whoever obtains a majority on the second vote is elected. They abolished that, because for obvious reasons it is unsatisfactory.
The next time they tried the second ballot they adopted a system whereby, if no one obtained a majority on the first ballot, then, on the second ballot ten days later they voted only on the two leading candidates on the first ballot. That has been unsatisfactory, also.
It will be observed that ten days later they held a second ballot. Now, some clever gentleman-he was clever; that is all-conceived the idea of doing all that balloting on the one day. His idea was not to have a second ballot, but to give the voter a second balloting or second choice at the same time.
The alternative vote is just a unique and freak system of voting. This is what Fischer Williams, one of the really great authorities in the world in respect to voting, says about the second ballot:
. No country which has tried the second ballot is content with it. Its evils have been one of the determining causes for the introduction and progress of proportional representation.
And at another page he says that the alternative vote, which succeeded the second ballot-
. . . though a great improvement in mechanism is still in principle only the second ballot in a new disguise.
That is all it is; it is just the second ballot in a new disguise. It allows the voter to vote twice or more on the same day by having a first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth or tenth choice, depending upon how many candidates there are in the field.
In an election where they have a choice like that the contest is not between parties. 
They do not concentrate on principles in an election like that. They say, Give me your first choice, vote for whomever you like on your second choice. The reason is that whoever gets the first choice, which is number one in the contingent or alternative vote-and its real name is the contingent vote-or in proportional representation, gets 79-66 per cent of the value of the ballot. The second choice is worth 17-33 per cent. So no candidate asks for the second choice, and much less would he ask for the third choice, because it is worth only a small fraction of the ballot.
The reason is that when a thinking voter goes into the polling booth his mind is made up. He is not a man who has a choice for this or that or anything else. He is not voting to have free water, or anything 1-ike that. His mind is made up to vote number one. But if his mind is not made up he would go in and vote number one and two, and, as I said a minute ago, the second choice is worth only 17-33 per cent of the value of the vote.
The contest becomes not an electoral contest, but rather a contest between candidates to try to obtain first choice. This alternative vote has been tried in quite a number of countries. It was recently bodily thrown out of Australia for federal senate elections, where it was a disastrous failure. In Australia, under the alternative vote, or the contingent vote as it is called, they elected their house of representatives. But they threw it out, and they now use another system. They elect their senate under the alternative vote. In recent years in Australia in an election they elected eighteen senators, three from each of six states. Eight hundred and sixty thousand votes elected seventeen senators-someone will say that is fair representation-and 820,000 votes elected one senator. Then, 178,000 did not elect any senators at all. There were three different parties.
All these freak systems of voting have many defects, and they all fail in practice. Someone has said that we must have electoral reform. It is not electoral reform we want. No electoral reform is superior to the one man, one vote majority system. When you go into the voting booth you know whom you are going to vote for, and you vote for him.
What we want and cannot get in this country, and perhaps for two or three more redistributions, is equal voting strength for every voter. For instance, in my riding with a population of approximately 70,000 there are about 45,000 voters. But I know of a riding with less than 20,000 population, and less than half of them vote. That is not fair representation.

I am going to say a word about the results of the alternative vote in Alberta. I am sorry to take so long, Mr. Chairman, and if I were in your place I would be tempted to call "Order". In the province of Alberta, in their last five general elections, there were 241 seats in the total, and in those 241 seats, on counting the second choices of the low candidate where it was necessary to do so, only six changes were made-six changes in 241 seats! That is a terrible price to put the province of Alberta to for such nonsense. If they had counted third, fourth and fifth choices it would have been even worse. In Pincher Creek, Alberta, three men were running. H. Bossenberry, Liberal; E. G. Cook, U.F.A.; R. O. Allison, Conservative. Bossenberry got 592 first-choice votes; Cook, 542, and Allison, 471. Not one of them got an absolute majority. So they counted the ballots of the low man over again, and the majority of the second choices of Allison's votes went to Cook, who, although he was in a minority on the first count, was declared elected over the man who had got most votes on the first count. We do not want that kind of system in Canada. Had they counted the ballots of Bossenberry and Cook over again, there is no telling who would have been elected. That is why I say to the hon. member for Winnipeg South that the alternative vote does not elect anyone by absolute majority, unless he gets a majority on the first ballot or on the counting of all ballot second choices.

Those who advocate the alternative vote never tell you which system they want. There are five different systems of alternative voting. In Manitoba and Alberta you must vote for one candidate, but you do not have to vote for the others. That is outlawed in the United States. In Australia you had to vote for all the candidates. But that system has been thrown out of Australia. There are several different systems. Which system are you going to try to foist on this country? They must agree on something, and so they advocate the Alberta and Manitoba system, which calls for voting for one candidate only, and then you can do what you like with the others. That is outlawed in the state of Connecticut, in the state of Michigan, in the state of California, and I do not know in how many other states, because, according to the United States constitution, every vote must have the same value and it does not have the same value when in the one case you can vote for only one candidate, in another case you can vote for two, and in another case vote for three candidates or more. That makes a differentiation in the value of the votes, of one vote as against another. Therefore it is rightly outlawed, and it should be outlawed here.
The other system, the proportional transferable vote system is superior. It has some merit. But it, too, has been tried in many different places and thrown out; for instance, thrown out in Kalamazoo, Michigan; in New South Wales. Australia; in Toledo, in New York, in Cleveland and in Edmonton. It has been thrown out of Saskatoon, out of North Battleford. out of New Westminster, out of France and out o. many other places. Why do we want to bother with this thing, Mr. Chairman? Anybody going in to vote does not want to be pestered with one, two, three, four choices. I always know for whom I am going to vote. I am not going to vote for free trade and protection at the same time. The people should know for whom they are going to vote. I could go on indefinitely. I have a lot more to say but I shall keep it in case somebody else speaks on this matter.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN SALARY OF CHIEF ELECTORAL OFFICER
speechtext:
I am sure it must be very interesting for those of us who come from Alberta to find how badly our system is working. As a matter of fact, I know of no one in Alberta who thinks it is working badly. But perhaps it is necessary for us to come here and listen to the experts tell us that we are all crazy and that we do not know what we are doing. However, we shall 
plod along in our own usual way, in spite of the experts and the kindly advice that we get here. I think it cannot be said of me, in any event, that I have become concerned because of recent political events in the elections in the Dominion of Canada and in the province of Alberta, because I did, standing where I now am, advocate this system of voting long before any of those elections were ever thought of.
I want to put this to hon. members, because we now have all these fractions, 70 odd per cent, 17 per cent and so on introduced, and I make this broad statement. Except for those of us who were nominated by acclamation by our parties, or w'here there was only a two-person contest, we were all nominated by the very principle embodied in the single transferable vote. In other words, if four people stand for nomination at a convention of any of our parties, the system invariably adopted is that the low man drops. We vote again and the next man drops, and we vote again until some person has received a minimum of 50 per cent, plus one vote of those in attendance. It might be said that you will get more than 50 per cent. Yes, you do. Therefore I emphasize the word "minimum". That is what the single transferable vote is, although in this case you have a ballot given you which gives you those alternative choices, without going through four or five votings as we do in any party convention that any of us have ever attended. That is the principle of the single transferable vote. It undertakes that all persons voting have a choice between the last two persons to be voted on. That is what it is. It means that every person voting has a choice between the winner and the runner-up. Can anyone suggest anything wrong with it? I do nor. mean these complicated fractions and percentages; but if we reduce the thing to its bones, to its very simple form, that is exactly what it is.
I do not intend to discuss or compare proportional representation with the single transferable vote. It does not apply to the same circumstances at all. Proportional representation is used only where you have a multiple-member constituency. The best example is any city which has not adopted the ward system. We heard that it was thrown out of here and thrown out of there. The answer is that the burghers and the voters of that city went back to the ward system and preferred to elect their members by that method. I will go along with my hon. friends over here that in multiple constituencies it does guarantee that the minorities have representation. I am not quarreling with that, We have it in our city, but it is something which is complicated. '

Dominion Elections Act
What I am so anxious to make plain tonight is that what those of us who favour this are seeking is simply that the person who comes here-I am a minority representative from Calgary West, and 148 others of us are in the same position-will undertake that when we come to parliament we shall have a majority of the persons who vote voting for us as against our nearest and our last opponent. That is what this thing is, and it means nothing more than that. It is not complicated in any sense whatever, except to give every voter a choice between the last two persons, exactly as is done in the conventions where we are nominated by our parties to run for office in this dominion parliament.
I want to use the illustration used by my honourable, able and kindly friend, the hon. member for Davenport, who got annoyed at me a moment ago. In the constituency of Fincher Creek there were three men running, Cook, Bossenberry and Allison. On the first count neither of the three had a majority. Then Allison, who, I think, belonged to my party-I am not sure-had the lowest number of votes of the three. In the meantime, as the hon. member for Davenport said, Bossenberry was running ahead of Cook. But when they counted the No. 2 votes of Allison, who dropped out, it meant that Cook had beaten Bossenberry, and it meant taking the minority man and giving him the majority. Why should that not be? The decision was then between Cook and Bossenberry, and the majority of the voters wanted Cook.
How can we here who believe in democracy and who do much talking about majority rule, conceding that to be the principle upon which we operate in a democracy, quarrel with the idea that the persons who come here should have a majority of the votes of the persons who are sufficiently interested to vote? How anyone who believes in democracy can put up an argument against that is quite beyond me. I think the difficulty is this, Mr. Chairman. You have heard of our province, I am quite sure, starting some rather original things politically and in many other ways. It is so easy at a distance to say we have that crazy system of the single transferable vote. I have talked to a goodly number of members privately about this matter. I say it is not blameworthy on their part, but I found a number whom one might think would think otherwise who simply did not understand the system. It is the simplest thing in the world. I guarantee one thing, namely, that he who represents the people of a constituency will be sent here to represent them by a majority of the people in that constituency, and it means nothing else.

I am glad to know there are so many members who are interested in the way
in which Canadians vote. I think the privilege of the ballot is being abused, and before it is too late we should have some reform in the method of voting. I do not think the majority of the people are satisfied with the single "X" marked on the ballot. I am sure that when the single transferable vote is properly explained to them we shall have no trouble whatever in canying that system into effect.. I wish to give notice now that at the next session I intend to introduce a bill dealing with this matter. If it should so happen that I am not returned at the next election I have no doubt there will be somebody else here who will take steps to introduce legislation to bring about the desired result, I hear a C.C.F. member saying something under his breath. I have nothing to fear from that quarter, when a C.C.F. candidate loses his deposit in my constituency.

I wish to bring to the attention of the minister a matter in which my riding is interested. In that riding, and I suppose in many others, there are certain governmental institutions-I am referring particularly to Westminster hospital- and from time to time employees of that institution, sometimes transient employees who have been there for only a short time, perhaps three months, become a charge upon the township. During all their lifetime they have not contributed one cent of taxes to the municipality, but they become a charge upon it. I understand that in the case of Chalk river, the municipality was not able

to carry the burden of this hospitalization and care of transient labotir that came in to build up the Chalk river plant.

No. The point I am coming at is this. While Westminster hospital does not come under the minister's department, the Prime Minister has proclaimed a great health scheme for the dominion. If it is to be as far-reaching as we are led to believe it is to be, surely a place for it to be made operative is where municipalities do not receive any taxes from these government institutions, but are required to take care of their employees. For instance, if a corporation of some kind had a business employing as many people, with as many millions of dollars invested in it as are invested in Westminster hospital, it would be contributing a large sum of money to the municipality by way of taxes. Not only that, but some of the people who are employed in this hospital send their children to the schools in the municipality. Yet in 1946 all the taxes the municipality of Westminster received from the hospital was $161 and some cents. Some provision should be made in cases like that particularly.
I know of several cases in which employees have contracted tubercular diseases, and it has been necessary for them to receive care at the sanitarium. Then, after they were discharged from the sanitarium, they required further care for some time while they were at their homes. This has become a burden on some of the municipalities. In this health plan the Prime Minister is bringing before the country, surely there is some way whereby that matter could be taken care of. I should like to hear what the minister has to say about it.

I may tell the minister that the distinction between health and welfare is very subtle. The cases to which I wish to refer are those people who suffer from infirmities. They must come to health to enjoy welfare. I wonder if the department has established a line of demarcation between health and welfare that is easy to understand. To me the two words are synonymous. Some of the experts on health may be experts on welfare, and vice versa. If there are doctors in the health branch administration and doctors in the welfare branch administration, they all must have made the same studies and reached the same results-to protect the health of the people. Welfare is not intended to make people rich; it is intended to make them healthy. I do not know whether I shall be here when the other item will be up, and I should like to submit this in all friendliness to the committee.
Family allowances come under welfare, because they are paid for young children who may or may not be in good health. Those allowances are paid according to age, but those who are sick do not receive any more than those who are well. The rate is standard
Supply-Health and Weljare

for all. That may be called welfare. Old people receive old age pensions, not because they are sick but because they have reached a certain age and are in need. The case I want to bring to the attention of the committee is that of people who suffer from infirmities.
These people are not exceedingly numerous and there would not be more than a few thousand in Canada. They suffer from disabilities and deficiencies which make life much harder for them. Nothing is provided for their assistance. The other day the hon. member for Macleod made a remarkable speech about incurables. There is a gap in our social service system. We hear a lot about social service; everybody is talking about it, and everybody thinks the government has a horn of plenty to satisfy the needs of all.
Old people may receive something if they are needy and are over the age of seventy years. The young receive something until they reach the age of sixteen years. The blind are assisted between the ages of twenty-one and seventy years. Along with the blind who are not between the ages of sixteen and twenty-one, those who suffer from infirmities receive no assistance from the ages of sixteen to seventy years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: They do in British Columbia.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I accept what my hon. friend says about British Columbia, but I do not know whether it is done in any other province. The hon. member for Terrebonne and the hon. member for Compton placed resolutions on the order paper to provide assistance for those between the ages of sixteen and seventy years who were suffering disabilities. They felt that the state should come to the assistance of those who could not look after themselves. If we accept the principle that the community must come to the assistance of its members who need it, why overlook the neediest cases? Just about a month before Christmas the great New York paper, the New York Times, devotes its front page to describing the neediest cases in the city. Some of those cases come under welfare, while others are health cases.
I had a survey made by the health unit of my constituency-this should be made in every constituency in the country-to find out those who needed the help of the state but could not reach the state, either because they lived in the back country and were not in contact with the authorities, because they were too shy to leave their homes, or for other reasons. These people all deserved special consideration. For a time this type of person was looked after by private charity. Private charity has

accomplished marvels in this country. One has only to note the magnificent institutions erected in our cities and towns by private charity for the welfare of our fellow citizens.
But taxes are high and those who are ready to give sometimes find that they cannot give as much, because it is hard for them to make both ends meet. If we accept the principle that the state must help those for whom private charity can no longer provide, we must first look after those whom we might term the deserted of life, les desherites de la vie. These people do not have the same standard of living as the average Canadian citizen because of their disability or handicap which prevents them from earning a living for themselves and their families. And two or three years-if I remember correctly it was in 1945; it was either 1945 or 1946-

I know it was a good debate, except for one speech, and that was the speech of the then minister of national health and welfare, the predecessor of my hon. friend the present minister. I was scandalized when I heard him say it was impossible to provide anything for the assistance of those who suffer from personal disability. I was both scandalized and shocked. I said it the other day. Hansard has reported me differently; but this is what I said; I was heard to say it, and I repeat it:	How is it that we
can send $20,000,000 to the children of Europe, but we cannot provide for our own people who are sick, who have not the means to go to the hospital and who have not the means to recuperate? What an absurdity!
I am all for helping those in other countries who are suffering; but how is it that we keep black spots in each constituency of this country? I could read the figures for my constituency. They are sad, but they are no sadder than those of any other constituency. They are the same. There are dwarfs in any constituency. There are people who have

Supply-Health and Welfare
lost their hands in sawmill accidents. Even sometimes in sliding they have broken legs or arms. Sometimes sports are responsible for these human deficiencies.
When people are poor and live in large families they cannot attend so well to those who have suffered. Those people should be given at least the same as is paid to the aged, because they suffer deficiencies that are sometimes worse than those suffered by the old people. That is easy to understand. But when I heard a minister of the crown daring to say in the House of Commons that the country had not enough money to look after those people I was most indignant.
I appeal to the good heart of the present Minister of National Health and Welfare. I hope he will not wait for the millennium to correct that absurd situation. This is the time to do something. It is most urgent because, when an injustice exists somewhere, whether we call it a social injustice or just an injustice, we should attend to it. I cannot see the difference between social justice and justice. When justice exists it is social justice. It is not necessary to use the word "social," because it is just justice. And when injustice exists it is not only injustice but social injustice.
When we think of any country with natural resources in the abundance in which we have them, a country in which there are people who suffer and who are ignored completely by the state, one is reminded of the parable of the good Samaritan. So many passed by and paid no attention to the man who was lying sick along the roadside. They were passing by, giving him the cold shoulder.
Those people may not be well enough to vote; they may not be able to leave their homes. Sometimes they cannot, because they have not the means to buy proper clothing to protect them against the rigours of our winter climate. Sometimes they cannot go out, because they are too sick and are unable to walk. Sometimes they are ashamed of their disabilities and do not leave their homes, because they would feel uncomfortable in meeting other people.
I must praise highly the health units of the province of Quebec which have accomplished marvels in our part of the country.
